Date of Discovery: This latest edition of the Ransomware Roundup covers the Inlock ransomware and a new variant of the Xorist ransomware that appears to target Cuba.
Method of Attack: Encrypts files on the compromised machine and demands ransom for file decryption
The Inlock ransomware encrypts files, changes the desktop wallpaper, and leaves a ransom note titled READ_IT.txt with a ransom message in Spanish.
The Xorist ransomware variant encrypts files, replaces the desktop wallpaper with a ransom message, includes a QR code with the attacker’s Bitcoin wallet address, and demands $100 worth of Bitcoin.
Attack Vector: Not explicitly mentioned for Inlock; however, it is known to spread via methods common to ransomware.

For the Xorist variant, the attack vector involves a fake PDF file named 'Ley del Presidente y Vicepresidente de la República de Cuba.pdf.exe', which tricks victims into thinking they have opened a legitimate document issued by the Cuban government.
Indicators of Compromise: Files encrypted with a “.inlock” file extension
Changed desktop wallpaper in Inlock ransomware
Executable file named 'Ley del Presidente y Vicepresidente de la República de Cuba.pdf.exe'
Benign PDF file labeled as the 'Official Gazette of the Republic of Cuba' with a parent self-extracting .rar file designed to launch a missing 'You Are Hacked.exe' application
Ransom note in Spanish with QR code for Bitcoin payment
